metrics.label: Employment in the most AI-exposed jobs, workers aged 22–25, year on year (September 2026)
Same age group, least AI-exposed jobs
Consecutive months of year-over-year decline in that first figure
Entry-level share of postings in the most exposed roles, 2021 to 2026

claims.text: In the year to September 2026, employment in the most AI-exposed US occupations fell 0.5% while the least-exposed grew 1.0%. For workers aged 22–25 the exposed group fell 3.7% and the least-exposed group rose 0.2%.

September was the 36th consecutive month of year-over-year decline for 22–25-year-olds in highly exposed occupations, a run that began in October 2023. For workers aged 26–30 the exposed group is now 2.8% below a year earlier, against growth of 0.9% in the least-exposed group.

Early-career workers aged 22–25 in the most AI-exposed occupations sit 19% below their kept-pace path in the August 2026 revision of the Stanford paper. That is a level gap, not the 3.7% annual rate above, and the two cannot be added.

In France, permanent-contract hires for 21–29-year-olds in the most AI-exposed fifth of occupations were about 28% below their November 2022 level by March 2026, against 8% in the least-exposed fifth. Terminations fell by about 23% and 6%, so the adjustment is slower hiring and turnover rather than layoffs.
In the most exposed occupations the entry-level share of US postings fell from 29% to 10% between 2021 and 2026, while the senior share rose from 22% to 47%.
Customer service representatives are among the most affected occupations in Microsoft’s usage-based analysis of Copilot conversations.
